```{r}
#| label: load_libraries_data
#| echo: false
# Load libraries and data
library(tidyverse)
library(Seurat)

# Set seed
set.seed(123456789L)
# Turn off scientific notation
options(scipen = 999)

# Load sample metadata
df_meta <- read_tsv("data/samples.tsv")
```

Approximate time: 70 minutes

## Loading the dataset into Seurat

These samples were processed with 10X kits and were therefore processed with their propietary software. Here, we make use of two pipelines `cellranger-arc` and `cellranger multi` where the first processes RNA + ATAC and multi takes case of RNA + ADT.

TODO

Therefore, we will have two folders of results that we will eventually merged together into one singular Seurat object. 

**We will be starting with the ADT protein and RNA expression data for sample `PT1`.**

```{r}
#| label: assign_sample
# Sample of interest
sample <- "PT1"
```

### Load counts matrix

First we will load in the counts matrices from the `ADT` folder with the `Read10X()` function. When we investigate the two matrices stored, we can see that we have both the "Gene Expression" (RNA) and "Antibody Capture" (ADT) matrices. 

```{r}
#| label: load_counts
# Load raw counts data
counts <- Read10X(file.path("data", sample, "ADT"))
names(counts)
```

Seurat allows you to have `Assays()` where we can store different matrices for the same cells within a single object. To initialize our Seurat object, let us first use the `CreateSeuratObject()` function for the RNA expression. Note that we set `assay = "RNA"`, which means that we can use the key "RNA" any time we want to look at the RNA expression over the protein or ATAC values.

```{r}
#| label: intialize_seurat
# RNA expression matrix
counts_gex <- counts[["Gene Expression"]]

# Create seurat object
seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = counts_gex,
  assay = "RNA",
  project = sample)

seurat
```

Now we can see that we have created a Seurat object with `r ncol(seurat)` cells and `r nrow(seurat)` genes within the assay `RNA`.

### Hashtags

```{r}
#| label: adt_counts
# Protein expression matrix (ADT and HTO)
counts_adt <- counts[["Antibody Capture"]]
```

We can take a look at all the proteins included in our experiment by looking at the rownames of our counts matrix. In particular we are looking for any "protein" that begins with `hashtag`. Some runs are comprised of [multiple, pooled samples that are tagged with specific antibodies](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-018-1603-1). The way to identify which sample a cell comes from is to use these sequences to **demultiplex**. The first thing we are going to do here is pull out those antibodies and match them.

```{r}
#| label: hash_metadata
#| eval: false
# Map of hash to patient
df_hash <- read.csv(file.path("data",
                              sample,
                              "ADT", "hashing_info.txt.gz"),
                    header = FALSE, sep = ":",
                    col.names = c("hash", "patient")) %>%
  # data wrangling
  mutate(hash = str_replace(hash, "H", "h"),
         hash = str_replace(hash, " ", ""))
df_hash
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hash_metadata
#| tbl-cap: Table of hashing information for each patient.
#| echo: false
# Map of hash to patient
df_hash <- read.csv(file.path("data",
                              sample,
                              "ADT", "hashing_info.txt.gz"),
                    header = FALSE, sep = ":",
                    col.names = c("hash", "patient")) %>%
  # data wrangling
  mutate(hash = str_replace(hash, "H", "h"),
         hash = str_replace(hash, " ", ""))

df_hash %>% knitr::kable()
```

The rownames of the matrix are the names of proteins and hashes, which we can see by looking at the first few proteins in the array:

```{r}
#| label: protein_names
# View first few protein names
rownames(counts_adt) %>% head()
```

All the proteins have the string `_TotalA` appended, so we are going to remove it for easy searching now and in the future. Once we accomplish that, we can search for the hashes in the array by searching for the string `hashtag`. 

```{r}
#| label: hashtag_search
# Remove appended _TotalA string from protein names
rownames(counts_adt) <- str_replace_all(rownames(counts_adt), "_TotalA", "")

# Looking for hashes in the dataset
hashes <- rownames(counts_adt)[str_detect(rownames(counts_adt), "hashtag")]
hashes
```

::: callout-note
# More hashes than expected
In the metadata, we see that there should only be 3 hashes, but we have 8 in our matrix. This is because the sequence for multiple hashes was included in the reference and does not effect the future results. 

So we will remove the irrelevant hashes from our counts matrix.
:::

Now that we have the names for each hash, we can pull those antibody captures out and store it as `HTO` in our Seurat object with the `CreateAssayObject()` function.

```{r}
#| label: hto_assay
# Grab counts for just the hashes
counts_hash <- counts_adt[df_hash$hash, ]

# Add HTO assay to our seurat object
seurat[["HTO"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = counts_hash)
seurat
```

To confirm that we added the `HTO` assay succesfully, we can check that the are 8 `Features()` in the assay - which should correspond to each of the hashes.

```{r}
#| label: hto_features
# Name of features in the HTO assay
Features(seurat[["HTO"]])
```

### Protein expression

Now that we have identified the hashes, we can proceed by adding the protein expression to our Seurat object. 

```{r}
#| label: counts_protein
# Protein expression
counts_protein <- counts_adt[!rownames(counts_adt) %in% hashes, ]
seurat[["ADT"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = counts_protein)

seurat
```

So now we have the RNA, HTO, and ADT assays in our Seurat object. We could also add the ATAC assay, however we will focus on the steps to do so in a future lesson.

Therefore, we can move forward with the next step of demultiplexing.

## Demultiplexing

In this step we will use the counts for each hashtag in the dataset to map each cell to the patient it belongs to.

```{r}
#| label: set_DefaultAssay
# Set default assay to HTO
DefaultAssay(seurat) <- "HTO"
```

TODO By default we have several metrics computed

```{r}
#| label: default_meta
#| eval: false
# Seurat metadata
seurat@meta.data %>% head()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-default_meta
#| tbl-cap: Metadata generated by default after adding `Assays()`
#| echo: false
# Seurat metadata
seurat@meta.data %>% head() %>% knitr::kable()
```

### Filtration

At this point it is quite evident that we have a lot of low quality cells or empty droplets. To improve the process of demultiplexing and reduce the number of computations 

First, we can take a look at the number of total counts associated with each cell to remove cells that have too few counts for the antibody to cleanly assign a sample identity. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-nCount_HTO
#| fig-cap: Histogram of hash counts per cell.
#| fig-width: 9
ggplot(seurat@meta.data) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = nCount_HTO),
                 fill = "lightblue",
                 bins = 100) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  theme_bw() + NoLegend() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 30)
```

The black line is drawn at `nCount_HTO = 30` to show the threshold we will be using to remove empty droplets. Following the methods section from the [Methods section of the paper](https://www.cell.com/immunity/fulltext/S1074-7613(25)00331-0), we will also remove RNA UMI counts ≤ 500 or ≥ 10,000.

```{r}
#| label: filter
# Filter based on HTO counts
seurat <- subset(seurat, nCount_HTO > 30)
# Filter based on RNA counts
seurat <- subset(seurat, nCount_RNA >= 500)
seurat <- subset(seurat, nCount_RNA <= 10000)
seurat
```

### Normalization

`NormalizeData()`: Normalize antibody counts with `normalization.method = "CLR"` (Centered Log-Ratio) and `margin = 2` (each cell is normalized across its hashtags).

TODO describe this method in more depth

```{r}
#| label: hto_norm
# CLR HTO normalization
seurat <- NormalizeData(
    seurat,
    assay = "HTO",
    normalization.method = "CLR",
    margin = 2
  )

seurat
```

With these normalized counts, we can start to see if we can clearly identify cells that have high expression of a singular hash.

### k-medoids demultiplexing

`HTODemux()`: Run k-medoids clustering with `positive.quantile = 0.95` to set a quantile threshold of 95% for a confident demultiplexing call.

::: callout-note
# TODO
https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/hashing_vignette.html

The demultiplexing function HTODemux() implements the following procedure:
We perform a k-medoid clustering on the normalized HTO values, which initially separates cells into K(# of samples)+1 clusters.
We calculate a ‘negative’ distribution for HTO. For each HTO, we use the cluster with the lowest average value as the negative group.
For each HTO, we fit a negative binomial distribution to the negative cluster. We use the 0.99 quantile of this distribution as a threshold.
Based on these thresholds, each cell is classified as positive or negative for each HTO.
Cells that are positive for more than one HTOs are annotated as doublets.

:::

::: callout-important
# figure of k-medoids
goes here
:::

```{r}
#| label: HTODemux
# HTO demultiplexing
seurat <- HTODemux(
    seurat,
    assay = "HTO",
    positive.quantile = 0.99,
    verbose = TRUE)
```

The results of this function call are stored in our `@meta.data`.

```{r}
#| label: demux_meta
#| eval: false
# Seurat metadata
seurat@meta.data %>% head()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demux_meta
#| tbl-cap: Metadata after running `HTODemux()` to demultiplex pooled cells.
#| echo: false
# Seurat metadata
seurat@meta.data %>% head() %>% knitr::kable()
```

`HTODemux` added the last six columns (17–21 in your list, plus `HTO_maxID` at 16):

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `HTO_maxID` | The hashtag with the **highest** normalised signal in that cell, whether or not it passed the threshold. |
| `HTO_secondID` | The hashtag with the **second-highest** signal. Useful for seeing which two donors a doublet came from. |
| `HTO_margin` | The difference between the top and second hashtag's normalised (CLR) values. Large means one hashtag clearly dominates; small means the cell is ambiguous. |
| `HTO_classification` | The detailed call. A singlet gets one hashtag name (`hashtag2`), a doublet gets both joined with `_` (`hashtag1_hashtag3`), and a cell with no hashtag above threshold gets `Negative`. |
| `HTO_classification.global` | The detailed call collapsed into three groups: `Singlet`, `Doublet` or `Negative`. Filter on this one. |
| `hash.ID` | The final per-cell label: the hashtag name for singlets, and `Doublet` or `Negative` otherwise. `HTODemux` also sets the object's active identities to this. |


From this, we can count how many cells belong to each patient:

```{r}
#| label: fig-nCells_hash.ID
#| fig-cap: Number of cells per demultiplexed hash ID.
#| fig-width: 10
# Number of cells per demultiplexed hash ID
ggplot(seurat@meta.data) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = hash.ID,
               fill = hash.ID),
           color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(x = hash.ID,
                label = after_stat(count)),
          stat = "count", vjust = -0.5,
          size = 3) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

The majority of our remaining cells are identified as `Negative`, meaning that a conclusive label was unable to be determined from the data. These cells are typically empty or filled with ambient RNA and some hash counts. To evaluate if we truly believe these are low-quality cells to remove, we can assess the `nCount_HTO` to see how many hash counts are present in those cells. If the levels are very low, we will be unable to identify which patient the cell comes from, and therefore remove them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nCount_HTO_vln
#| fig-cap: Distribution of hash counts, grouped by demultipled hash IDs.
# Distribution of HTO counts per demultiplexed hash ID
VlnPlot(seurat,
        features = "nCount_HTO",
        group.by = "hash.ID",
        assay = "HTO",
        pt.size = 0) +
  scale_y_log10()
```

We can see why the cells that were called `Negative` received that label from the violin plot. Each cell had very low levels of hash expression, meaning that no algorithm would be able to confidently map the cell to a label.

We can also see patterns of expression for each hash across the identities. We are ideally looking for peaks of zero expression for hashes other than the `hash.ID`, indicating that the cell has high levels of the `hash.ID` hash.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hto_ridge
#| fig-cap: Ridge plot of HTO normalized expression for each hash.
#| fig-width: 9
# HTO expression by demultiplexed hash ID
RidgePlot(
  seurat,
  features = df_hash$hash,
  group.by = "hash.ID",
  assay = "HTO")
```

Which is exactly what we see in the `RidgePlot()`.

### Removing doublets and negative

Now that we are confident in our demultiplexed calls, we can remove the identified `doublets` and `negative` cells. These will only introduce noise into the dataset so we will remove them from our analysis.

```{r}
#| label: filter_doublets_negatives
# Remove doublets and negatives
seurat_demux <- subset(seurat, subset = (hash.ID %in% df_hash$hash))
seurat_demux
```

And now we can take the mapping of `hash` to `patient` and add it to the metadata of our `Seurat` object. This way, moving forward, we are able to associate each cell with a specific patient. We will do a `left_join()` of to merge together this information.

```{r}
#| label: map_hash_patient
# Add patient to metadata by matching hash
meta <- left_join(seurat_demux@meta.data,
                  df_hash, by = c("hash.ID" = "hash"))
rownames(meta) <- Cells(seurat_demux)

seurat_demux@meta.data <- meta
```

Oftentimes when you run `left_join()` of dataframes, you lose the  rownames of the original dataframe. If we were to put this back into the `Seurat` object without the cell barcodes, we would get many errors in future steps. Hence why we explicitly set the `rownames(meta)` as a secondary step.

# Loading processed seurat object

Now that we understand the basics of how demultiplexing works, we can go back to the full dataset which contains all our samples. To save time and computation, we have generated the merged and demultiplexed seurat object for you to load into your R session.

```{r}
#| label: load_seurat_demux
# Load the processed seurat object
seurat_demux <- readRDS("data/processed_seurat_objects/seurat_demux.RDS")
seurat_demux
```

For more information on how this object was created, we have created a detailed [lesson](Aside_gen_pooled_seurat.qmd) on how each sample was loaded in an automated fashion with a `for` loop. The `RNA` assay was also processed following a standard scRNA-seq workflow.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
# RNA processing code

After merging together each sample, these were the following steps that were performed on the `RNA` assay:

```{r}
#| label: process_rna
#| eval: false
### Process RNA
DefaultAssay(seurat) <- "RNA"
seurat <- NormalizeData(seurat)
seurat <- FindVariableFeatures(seurat, nfeatures = 2000)
seurat <- ScaleData(seurat)
seurat <- RunPCA(seurat, npcs = 50, reduction.name = "pca_rna", verbose = FALSE)

seurat <- RunHarmony(seurat, group.by.vars = "orig.ident",
                     reduction.use = "pca_rna", dims.use = 1:30,
                     reduction.save = "harmony_rna", verbose = FALSE)
seurat <- RunUMAP(seurat, reduction = "harmony_rna", dims = 1:30,
                  reduction.name = "umap_rna", reduction.key = "rnaUMAP_",
                  verbose = FALSE, seed.use = 123456789L)

seurat <- FindNeighbors(seurat, reduction = "harmony_rna", dims = 1:30,
                        graph.name = c("nn_rna", "snn_rna"))
seurat <- FindClusters(seurat, graph.name = "snn_rna", resolution = 0.8, 
                       algorithm = 4, random.seed = 123456789L)
```

:::

As a starting point to better understand the dataset that we loaded, we can assess how many cells we have per patient.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nCells_patient
#| fig-cap: Number of cells per patient in the full dataset.
#| fig-width: 10
# Number of cells per patient
ggplot(seurat_demux@meta.data) +
  geom_bar(aes(x = patient,
               fill = hiv_status),
           color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(x = patient,
                label = after_stat(count)),
          stat = "count", vjust = -0.5,
          size = 3) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```
